title: First Humans in Space
summary: First, two brave dogs and a chimpanzee showed that living things could ride a rocket and come home. Then, in 1961, a young pilot called Yuri Gagarin shouted 'Let's go!' and became the first person ever to fly around the Earth. Soon after came the first American astronauts, the first woman in space, and a cosmonaut who floated outside his spaceship on a rope.

sections.heading: Test Pilots with Fur
paragraphs: By 1960 rockets could reach orbit, but nobody knew for sure what would happen to a living body up there. Could a person swallow without gravity pulling food down? Would the heart beat normally? Would the brain get confused and the person faint? Doctors on both sides of the Cold War had worried guesses but no answers. So before any human climbed aboard, animals went first.

Remember Laika from the last chapters: she reached orbit in 1957, but her spacecraft was never built to come back. The next big step was to send animals into orbit AND bring them home safely. The Soviet Union tried this with a new spaceship called Vostok, the very same design that would later carry a human. The first attempt, in July 1960, ended badly when the rocket failed shortly after launch and the two dogs on board were killed. The engineers fixed the problem and tried again.

On 19 August 1960 a rocket lifted off from the Baikonur launch site in Kazakhstan carrying two small, light-coloured dogs named Belka ('Whitey') and Strelka ('Little Arrow'). They were not alone. The capsule was a tiny zoo: dozens of mice, two rats, insects and even plants rode along so scientists could study how different kinds of life coped with spaceflight. A television camera pointed at the dogs, so the controllers could actually watch them float in their harnesses.

The film showed something worrying. During the fourth trip around the Earth, one dog became sick and seemed very uncomfortable. That small detail mattered enormously: it was one reason Soviet planners decided to keep the first human flight short, in case people also felt ill. About 25 hours after launch, on 20 August 1960, the capsule came back through the atmosphere and the dogs landed safely. Belka and Strelka were the first animals to go into orbit and return alive. They became celebrities, appearing on stamps, postcards and toys. Later Strelka had puppies, and one of them, named Pushinka ('Fluffy'), was sent as a friendly gift from the Soviet leader to the family of the American president, John F. Kennedy, in the middle of the Cold War.

The Americans used a different animal. Because chimpanzees are our close relatives, US scientists believed they would be a good stand-in for a human pilot. A young chimp named Ham had been trained for months to pull levers when a light flashed; if he did it right, he got a banana pellet. On 31 January 1961 Ham rode a Mercury capsule on top of a Redstone rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida. This was not an orbital flight but a suborbital one: a giant arc up into space and back down into the ocean, like a ball thrown extremely high.

Ham's flight was rough. The rocket flew faster and farther than planned, and his capsule came down about 210 km (130 miles) beyond the target point. The cabin also lost air pressure, but Ham was sealed inside his own pressurized couch and was fine. Most importantly, he kept pulling his levers correctly while weightless, showing that a pilot could think and work in space. After about 16 and a half minutes he splashed into the Atlantic, and a helicopter picked him up. Ham later lived at the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., and at a zoo in North Carolina, and died in 1983 at about 25 years old.

sections.heading: The Boy from Klushino
paragraphs: Yuri Alekseyevich Gagarin was born on 9 March 1934 in the village of Klushino, west of Moscow. His father was a carpenter and his mother worked on the village's collective farm. When Yuri was seven, the Second World War reached his village and it was occupied by the German army. His family was pushed out of their house and lived for a time in a dugout, a hole in the ground with a roof. It was a hard, frightened childhood, and when the war ended he went back to school hungry for a better life.

As a teenager Gagarin trained as a foundry worker, learning to pour hot metal into moulds, and then studied at a technical college in the city of Saratov on the Volga River. There he joined a local flying club and discovered that he loved being in the air. The air force noticed him. He trained as a military pilot, graduated in 1957 (the year of Sputnik) and flew jet fighters in the far north of Russia, near the Arctic Circle, where winter nights last for weeks.

In 1959 Soviet doctors secretly began searching the air force for possible 'cosmonauts', a Russian word meaning 'sailors of the universe'. They wanted young, healthy pilots who were calm under stress, and they also wanted SMALL ones, because the Vostok cabin was cramped. Gagarin was only about 1.57 m (5 ft 2 in) tall. In 1960 he became one of 20 men chosen for training. They spun in centrifuges (machines that whirl you around to imitate the heavy push of launch), sat for days in silent, sealed rooms, jumped with parachutes and studied the spacecraft.

Gagarin was quick, cheerful and friendly, with a famous wide smile. Sergei Korolev, the secret Chief Designer you met in earlier chapters, liked him a great deal. In the end two men were the leading candidates: Gagarin and Gherman Titov. A few days before launch, Gagarin was picked for the first flight, with Titov as his backup, ready to take his place if he fell ill.

The Vostok spacecraft he would ride was simple but clever. The crew part was a metal ball about 2.3 m wide, covered in a heat shield on all sides. Because it was a ball, it did not need to point in a particular direction when it came back through the air; its heavy bottom made it swing into the right position, like a weighted toy that always stands back up. Below the ball was an equipment section with the retrorocket (a braking rocket) and supplies. Inside, the cosmonaut sat on an ejection seat, a seat with its own small rockets that could shoot him out of the craft. The whole flight was designed to be controlled automatically from the ground, because no one knew whether a human could think clearly in weightlessness. Gagarin could take over by hand in an emergency, but the controls were locked with a secret code inside a sealed envelope.

sections.heading: Poyekhali! 108 Minutes Around the World
paragraphs: Early on the morning of 12 April 1961, Gagarin and Titov were woken, given breakfast and helped into their orange pressure suits. A bus drove them to the launch pad, where the tall R-7 rocket stood steaming in the cold spring air, its tanks full of kerosene and super-cold liquid oxygen. Gagarin rode a lift to the top, climbed into the Vostok ball and was strapped in. Korolev, who had hardly slept with worry, talked to him over the radio.

At 9:07 in the morning, Moscow time (06:07 UTC), the engines roared. As the rocket rose, Gagarin called out a cheerful word that became famous around the world: 'Poyekhali!', which means 'Let's go!' or 'Off we go!' Within minutes the strap-on boosters fell away, the core stage burned out, and the upper stage pushed him the rest of the way into orbit. He was now travelling at about 27,400 km/h, falling around the Earth just as Newton's cannonball does in the thought experiment from Part 10.

Gagarin became the first human to see the Earth from space. He reported the bright blue band of the atmosphere at the edge of the planet, the shadows of clouds and the dark sky. He ate and drank a little to show it was possible, tried writing notes in his logbook, and kept describing everything into his radio. He felt fine. Weightlessness, which doctors had feared, turned out to be strange but bearable.

His single lap around the planet took him across Siberia, the Pacific Ocean, the tip of South America and the South Atlantic. Over Africa the retrorocket fired to slow him down so he would fall back into the air. Then something went wrong. The equipment section was supposed to separate cleanly from the ball, but a bundle of cables kept the two pieces joined, and the spacecraft began to tumble. For several minutes Gagarin was spun around as he plunged into the atmosphere, until the heat burned through the cables and the ball broke free. He stayed calm and reported that things were all right.

Now came the part that was kept secret for years. Vostok's ball was too heavy to land gently on a parachute with a person inside; it would hit the ground very hard. So the plan had always been for the cosmonaut to leave it. At about 7 km above the ground the hatch blew off and Gagarin was shot out on his ejection seat. He then separated from the seat and floated down under his own parachute, while the empty capsule came down separately on its own parachute nearby.

He landed in a field near the city of Engels, in the Saratov region, not far from where he had learned to fly. A farm woman and her granddaughter saw a man in a bright orange suit and a white helmet walking towards them, and they were frightened. Gagarin reportedly called out that he was a friend, a Soviet citizen, and that he needed a telephone to call Moscow. From launch to landing the flight lasted about 108 minutes (later studies suggest the true figure may have been a minute or two less).

Why the secret? At the time, the rules of the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale (FAI), the organization that certifies flying records, said a pilot had to land inside his aircraft for a record to count. Soviet officials worried that the flight would not be accepted, and they also wanted the Vostok to look perfect. So for years they told the world Gagarin had landed in his capsule. Some early Soviet descriptions accidentally hinted at the truth, but the government did not officially admit the ejection until 1971. The FAI accepted the record anyway and later changed its rules, because the important thing was that a human had launched, orbited and returned safely.

sections.heading: A Hero Overnight
paragraphs: Gagarin left Moscow that morning as a senior lieutenant whom almost nobody had heard of. While he was still in orbit, he was promoted to major, and Soviet radio announced the flight to the world. Within hours his name and smiling face were on front pages from Tokyo to Buenos Aires. Two days later a huge crowd filled Red Square in Moscow to welcome him. In the following years he toured dozens of countries.

Gagarin himself never flew in space again. The Soviet leaders thought he was too precious a national hero to risk. He trained other cosmonauts, studied engineering and kept trying to get back onto the flight list. On 27 March 1968, he and an instructor, Vladimir Seryogin, were killed when their MiG-15 training jet crashed during a routine flight. He was only 34. Investigations have offered several possible causes, and historians still discuss them, but no single explanation has been fully proven.

sections.heading: America's Mercury Seven and Shepard's Hop
paragraphs: The United States had started its own human spaceflight programme, called Project Mercury, in 1958. Mercury was the messenger of the gods in Roman myths, a speedy name for a speedy craft. On 9 April 1959 NASA introduced its first astronauts to the public at a crowded press conference in Washington. There were seven, all military test pilots: Scott Carpenter, Gordon Cooper, John Glenn, Gus Grissom, Wally Schirra, Alan Shepard and Deke Slayton. They became known as the Mercury Seven, and almost overnight they were as famous as film stars.

On 5 May 1961, just over three weeks after Gagarin, Alan Shepard lay on his back in a capsule he had named Freedom 7, perched on a Redstone rocket at Cape Canaveral. The launch had already been postponed by bad weather, and that morning the countdown kept stopping for small problems. Shepard waited in the capsule for hours. Getting impatient, he is reported to have told the controllers to fix their little problem and 'light this candle'.

When the Redstone finally fired, it pushed him upwards with a force of about six times his normal weight. The flight was suborbital: he rose to about 187 km, well above the 100 km line many people use as the edge of space, and then curved back down. During about five minutes of weightlessness he became the first person to steer a spacecraft by hand, using a control stick to turn the capsule, and he looked out through a small periscope at the coast of Florida. On the way down the force pressing him into his couch reached about 11 times his weight for a few seconds.

Just over 15 minutes after launch, Freedom 7 splashed into the Atlantic about 487 km from the launch pad. A helicopter lifted Shepard and his capsule to the aircraft carrier USS Lake Champlain. His flight was much shorter than Gagarin's, and he never went into orbit, but millions of Americans had watched it live on television, and he became the first American in space. Ten years later, in 1971, Shepard would walk on the Moon with Apollo 14.

A second suborbital flight followed on 21 July 1961, when Gus Grissom flew Liberty Bell 7. After splashdown the hatch blew open too early, water poured in, and Grissom had to swim for his life while the capsule sank. He was rescued, but the capsule lay on the bottom of the Atlantic until it was found and raised in 1999.

sections.heading: Glenn, Friendship 7 and the Woman Who Checked the Numbers
paragraphs: A suborbital hop was not enough. To match Gagarin, an American needed to go all the way around the world, and the Redstone was not powerful enough. NASA switched to the much larger Atlas rocket, which was originally built as an intercontinental missile. The astronaut chosen was John Glenn, a Marine Corps pilot from Ohio who had flown in two wars and set a speed record by flying across the United States in under three and a half hours.

Before Glenn's flight, NASA had begun using electronic computers, such as the IBM 7090, to work out the path, or trajectory, of the capsule: exactly when to fire the retrorockets and where it would come down in the ocean. Computers were new, room-sized and sometimes made mistakes, and many people did not yet trust them. Glenn asked for the computer's numbers to be checked by a human expert. According to Katherine Johnson's own memory of it, he said to 'get the girl to check the numbers', and that if she said the numbers were good, he was ready to go.

'The girl' was Katherine Johnson, then about 43 and one of the best mathematicians at NASA's Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. Born in 1918 in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, she had been so quick at maths that she started high school at about ten. In 1953 she joined a group of Black women mathematicians at Langley known as 'computers', a job title in the days when a computer was a person who computed. At that time the American South was segregated: Black and white workers were kept apart in offices, cafeterias and even bathrooms. Johnson still earned the trust of the engineers by asking sharp questions and being right. She had already calculated the trajectory for Shepard's flight in 1961.

To check Glenn's orbit, Johnson worked through the same long equations by hand, using a desk calculating machine and pages of figures. The writer Margot Lee Shetterly, whose book 'Hidden Figures' made Johnson famous, says the work took about a day and a half. Her answers matched the computer's. Johnson later worked on the paths for the Apollo missions to the Moon, and in 2015 President Barack Obama gave her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest award for an American civilian. She died in 2020 at the age of 101.

After many delays for weather and equipment, Glenn launched in his capsule Friendship 7 on 20 February 1962. As the Atlas ignited, fellow astronaut Scott Carpenter said over the radio, 'Godspeed, John Glenn.' Glenn circled the Earth three times. He saw four sunsets and sunrises in less than five hours and reported a mystery: glowing specks floating around his capsule like fireflies. Later astronauts worked out that they were bits of frost flaking off the spacecraft and lit by the Sun.

Then came a scare. A signal on the ground suggested that Friendship 7's heat shield might have come loose. If it had, Glenn would burn up on re-entry. Mission controllers told him to keep the retrorocket pack, which was strapped over the heat shield, instead of throwing it away as planned, hoping its straps would hold the shield in place. As he dropped into the atmosphere, Glenn saw chunks of the burning pack fly past his window. It was frightening, but he came through safely. The signal turned out to be a faulty sensor; the shield had been fine all along.

Glenn splashed down in the Atlantic 4 hours, 55 minutes and 23 seconds after launch. He was the first American to orbit the Earth, and he was given a huge ticker-tape parade in New York City. He later became a United States senator, and in 1998, at the age of 77, he flew into space again on the Space Shuttle. His capsule, Friendship 7, is now on display at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

sections.heading: The Seagull: Valentina Tereshkova
paragraphs: In 1962 the Soviet Union quietly began training a group of women as cosmonauts. They were not chosen from pilots, because there were few women military pilots at the time. Instead the selectors looked for experienced parachutists, since a Vostok pilot had to eject and land by parachute. Five women were picked from hundreds of applicants.

One of them was Valentina Tereshkova, born on 6 March 1937 in a small village near the city of Yaroslavl, north-east of Moscow. Her father, a tractor driver, was killed in war when she was a toddler. She left school at about 16 to work, first in a tyre factory and then in a textile mill, weaving cloth, while studying in the evenings. In her spare time she joined a local flying club and made many parachute jumps. That hobby changed her life.

On 16 June 1963 Tereshkova launched aboard Vostok 6 and became the first woman in space. She was 26. Her radio call sign was 'Chaika', which means 'Seagull', and her words 'Ya Chaika' ('I am Seagull') became famous. Another cosmonaut, Valery Bykovsky, was already in orbit in Vostok 5, and the two spacecraft flew at the same time, with the pilots talking to each other by radio.

Tereshkova's flight was not a quick hop. She spent nearly three days in space, 2 days and almost 23 hours, and went around the Earth 48 times. That was more time in space than all the American Mercury astronauts had spent added together up to then. She took photographs of the horizon, which scientists used to study the layers of the atmosphere, and kept a logbook. She later said the flight was tiring and uncomfortable at times, which is not surprising: she was strapped into a cabin the size of a small cupboard for three days.

On 19 June, like every Vostok pilot, she ejected and landed by parachute. Tereshkova was made a Hero of the Soviet Union and became a famous public figure, an engineer and later a politician. She never flew in space again, and no other woman went into space for 19 years, until the Soviet cosmonaut Svetlana Savitskaya in 1982. Tereshkova is still the only woman ever to have flown a space mission completely alone.

sections.heading: Leonov Steps Outside
paragraphs: By 1965 people had spent days in space, but always sealed inside a capsule. To build stations or land on the Moon, someone would one day have to go outside and work. The Soviets wanted to try it first. Their spaceship, Voskhod 2, was an adapted Vostok with a clever addition: an inflatable tube called an airlock, named Volga, attached to the side. An airlock is a small room with two doors, so a person can leave a spacecraft without letting all the air out of the cabin. Once in orbit, the tube would blow up like a long balloon. The cosmonaut would climb in, close the inner door, let the air out of the tube, open the outer door and float into space.

The crew were commander Pavel Belyayev and Alexei Leonov, born in 1934 in a village in Siberia. Leonov was a fighter pilot and also a talented artist who loved to draw and paint. They launched on 18 March 1965. On their first orbit Leonov wriggled into the airlock and, at the end of a tether about 5 m long, pushed himself out of the hatch. He was the first human to float freely in space. Below him, he later said, he could see the Black Sea and the curve of the Earth. A camera filmed him tumbling slowly at the end of his line, high above the clouds.

Then came a dangerous problem. In the vacuum, Leonov's spacesuit swelled up like an overfilled balloon. The air pressure inside it pushed outward with nothing outside to push back, so the suit grew stiff and his hands and feet pulled back inside the gloves and boots. He could not reach the camera switch on his thigh, and, much worse, he could not fit back through the narrow airlock opening.

Leonov thought fast. Without asking ground control, he opened a valve and let some of the air out of his suit, lowering the pressure to below the safe limit. This was risky, because a sudden drop in pressure can cause the bends, a painful sickness divers can get. But it worked: the suit softened, and he pulled himself into the airlock head first instead of feet first as planned. Then he had to turn himself around inside the tight tube to close the hatch. By the time he got back into the cabin he was soaked in sweat and his heart was racing. He had been outside the spacecraft for about 12 minutes.

Voskhod 2's troubles were not over. The automatic landing system failed, so the crew had to steer and fire the retrorocket by hand, later than planned. They came down hundreds of kilometres off course, in a deep, snowy forest in the Ural Mountains near the city of Perm. Rescuers could see the capsule from a helicopter but could not land among the trees. The two cosmonauts spent a freezing night in the forest. Rescuers on skis reached them the next day, and after a second night in a log cabin, everyone skied out to a waiting helicopter.

Leonov's spacewalk was a world first, and it showed that people could leave their spacecraft, but it also showed how hard working outside would be. Less than three months later, in June 1965, the American astronaut Ed White made the first US spacewalk, and both countries kept learning how to design better suits. Leonov later flew again in 1975, and his paintings and drawings of space, including sketches he made in orbit, are among the first artworks made by someone who had actually been there.

Even so, the Soviet Union seemed to keep winning every first: first satellite, first man, first woman, first spacewalk. American leaders decided they needed a goal so huge that both countries would have to start almost from scratch. Just six weeks after Gagarin's flight, and only 20 days after Alan Shepard's 15-minute hop, President John F. Kennedy stood before the United States Congress on 25 May 1961 and made an astonishing promise. The country, he said, should commit itself to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth before the decade was out. At that moment, the total American experience of human spaceflight was about 15 minutes.

deepDive: Who really 'won' the early human spaceflight race depends on what you count, and historians still debate it. On paper the Soviet Union took nearly every early first, largely because Korolev's R-7 was far more powerful than any American rocket of the time. It could lift a Vostok of about 4.7 tonnes into orbit, while the Mercury capsule had to be kept well under 2 tonnes so the Atlas could carry it. Soviet secrecy also hid failures and shortcuts. Vostok had no backup retrorocket; instead, its orbit was chosen low enough that air drag would have brought it down within about ten days if the braking rocket failed, which is why it carried food and water for even longer than that. The cosmonauts ejected because the capsule's landing was too hard to survive inside, a fact hidden for a decade partly because of the FAI rule that a pilot had to land with his craft. Gagarin's flight time is itself a small puzzle: the official figure is 108 minutes, but later analyses of the timeline suggest about 106. Mercury took a different path. Its capsule was designed for a water landing with the pilot aboard, and its engineers added more manual control after the astronauts, all test pilots, insisted on being pilots and not passengers. Shepard's suborbital flight is sometimes dismissed, but it reached about 187 km, comfortably above the Kármán line, so it was a genuine spaceflight, just not an orbital one. Another debate concerns credit. For decades the women and Black mathematicians at Langley, such as Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson, were left out of the popular story; the 2016 book and film 'Hidden Figures' brought their work to wide attention, although the film simplified and moved some events for drama. Similarly, the Soviet female cosmonaut group was disbanded in 1969 without any of the others flying, and some historians argue Tereshkova's flight was partly a propaganda move rather than the start of real equality. Finally, the physical risks were real: Glenn's heat-shield alarm, Grissom's sinking capsule, Gagarin's tumbling re-entry and Leonov's ballooning suit all show how thin the margins were in these first years.
funFact: Valentina Tereshkova's three-day flight in 1963 lasted longer than all six crewed Mercury flights put together.
